description: We are Red Circle, a team from Douala Local Event, building an interactive Mars survival guide that maps real terrain, elevation, and weather hazards using NASA’s open data, so exploring Mars feels like planning a real journey. We're recruiting teammates with skills in web/app development (especially maps and geospatial tools like Leaflet.js, OpenLayers, or WMTS/WMS), UI/UX design, data visualization, and science storytelling. Anyone curious about space and real scientific data is invited to join.
summary: The Mars Survival Map by the Red Circle team is an interactive, two-scale web application built for the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge. A Site Map covers Jezero Crater at 4 m resolution, and a Planet Map screens the whole planet on a 30 km grid. It offers least-energy walking routes, hazard classes from slope and roughness, flat sites for habitats, and an EVA planner using computed solar geometry and MEDA temperatures. It is built from open NASA data and documented physics, and every metric is labelled “NASA data”, “Physics model” or “Team assumption”, so users can see exactly where each parameter comes from
details:
How It Works

The Mars Survival Map works at two scales, one for high-level site screening and one for granular surface operations. Both are built by an automated data pipeline from open NASA data .

At the Site scale (currently Jezero Crater, about 4 km across), the app processes a HiRISE Digital Terrain Model (DTM) at 4 m per pixel, with an optional 1 m native window and a 0.25 m HiRISE photo layer, to compute local slope and surface roughness. It uses documented physics models (Minetti 2002 for walking cost, adapted to Martian gravity with Cavagna 2000) to find the least-energy route between any two points with an A* search. It also identifies flat sites suitable for habitats (≤ 5° slope, ≤ 0.25 m roughness) and includes an Extravehicular Activity (EVA) outing planner that combines computed solar geometry (Allison & McEwen 2000) and local MEDA temperature data with a custom Mars local-time clock.

At the Planet scale, it provides a 0.5° grid (about 30 km) for site screening, combining global MOLA elevation, Odyssey neutron flux (a hydrogen proxy) and MGS TES thermal inertia, plus a modelled mean temperature. Every cell shows its data coverage, and missing layers are never filled with invented values.

Tools and Technologies

The project is a lightweight, static architecture, developed on modest hardware: a 2016 ThinkPad T460s (Intel Core i5-6200U, integrated graphics, about 20 GB RAM) running Ubuntu 24.04 with no GPU computing.

  • Data pipeline (backend): Python 3.12 (3.10+ supported) handles ingestion and processing. Custom scripts fetch only the needed window of large PDS3 DTMs using HTTP Range requests, process MEDA weather logs and assemble the planet grid. rasterio handles the geospatial data, with NumPy, Pillow and Requests.
  • Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS. Routing, line-of-sight and shadow computations run directly in the browser, in Web Workers, with terrain stored in compact packed binary files.
  • Visualization: Leaflet for 2D mapping and three.js for 3D terrain viewing.
  • Testing and deployment: pytest and Node.js tests check that the Python and JavaScript routing agree. The site is a static site on Vercel (default build settings: 2 vCPU, 8 GB build machine), with no serverless functions and no backend.
  • AI tools: the site icon was generated with AI (chatgpt image).

Benefits and Intended Impact

The tool bridges the gap between raw scientific data and actionable survival planning. For a future astronaut or mission planner, a short route isn’t enough: they need to know whether the terrain’s roughness and the energy it demands fit within the limits of a suit system. The map assumes a 170 kg suited astronaut with a 326 W metabolic budget, and it says so in the interface. By combining walking energy, hazards, time of day, temperature and sun exposure, it gives a transparent, evidence-based baseline for planning Martian surface operations.

The intended impact is to give the open-source and space-enthusiast community an accessible tool that puts hard data ahead of science-fiction tropes and is honest about its limits. We also hope it can be a modest contribution to Mars exploration, and we would be glad if NASA engineers and mission planners found any part of it useful.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Strict provenance tracking. Our design philosophy is total transparency. Any survival guide has to fill data gaps with models or assumptions, so the interface tags every metric with its origin: “NASA data” (e.g., elevation), “Physics model” (e.g., solar geometry, energy cost, planet-map temperature) or “Team assumption” (e.g., suit power limits, hazard thresholds, the 25% energy reserve). A Sources page documents every dataset: name, link, what we took and how it is used.

Performance under constraint. Rather than asking users to download a 130 MB DTM, we use HTTP Range requests in Python to extract only the window we need from NASA’s servers. The terrain is block-averaged to 4 m, stored as packed 16-bit and 8-bit files, and processed in background workers, so energy routing, line-of-sight and shadows run instantly in the browser without a backend server.

Open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/InputOutputStream/Mars-Survival-Map
